title: The Western Schism (1378–1417)
hook: rival popes, divided saints, forty confusing years

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine's Dialogue, a conversation with God about a broken road. Your line was christ is the bridge. What did you notice when you crossed one? Today closes the week. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

The pope is finally back in Rome. Catherine's letters, the long wait, the journey home: it's done. Then the pope dies, and the cardinals meet to choose the next one, with crowds in the streets outside shouting for a Roman, or at least an Italian. They elect a man who takes the name Urban the Sixth. Later, some of those same cardinals leave Rome, say the election was forced by the crowd, and choose someone else, who settles in Avignon. Now there are rival popes, each with his own cardinals, each sure he is the true successor of Peter. Today: the Western Schism.
screen: `BACK IN ROME, AT LAST.` → `A FRIGHTENED ELECTION.` → `RIVAL POPES.`

segments.voice: First, the split. A schism is a tear in the Church's unity, and this one ran right through the West. Kingdoms took sides. Some dioceses ended up with rival bishops. Ordinary Catholics, trying to be faithful, could not easily tell which pope was the real one, and honest people chose differently. Second, the saints. Catherine of Siena, whom we met this week, backed Urban in Rome with all her energy. Vincent Ferrer, a Dominican preacher later honored as a saint too, backed the Avignon line for years. Holy, prayerful people stood on opposite sides of the question. The facts were truly tangled, and Catholics today honor saints from both sides. Third, the attempted cure. A council met at Pisa to end the split, deposed the rival popes, and elected a new one. But the others refused to step down, and now there was one more claimant than before. Fourth, the end. Another council, at Constance, finally untangled it: one claimant resigned, the others were set aside, and a single pope, Martin the Fifth, was elected and accepted. Through all of it, Christians could pray the words Jesus prayed in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one." It's a prayer for unity, prayed by him, and it held even when Christians could not agree whom to follow.
screen: `ONE CHURCH, RIVAL POPES.` · `SAINTS ON BOTH SIDES.` · `A CURE THAT ADDS A CLAIMANT.` · `A COUNCIL AT CONSTANCE ENDS IT.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray through confusion. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you honestly can't figure out right now: a decision, a disagreement, a question about faith or family where good people see it differently. Don't try to solve it in the sit. Just hold it, without forcing an answer. If you pray, you can hold Jesus' words, that they all may be one, and ask for light. If you don't, simply let the confusion be there without fighting it, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Western Schism. The years when rival popes divided the Western Church and saints stood on both sides, until a council at Constance healed the split. Today's word.

Your line: even saints were confused. This week ran from the love that moves the sun, through no scapegoats, all shall be well, kept because loved, go back to Rome and the bridge, to here. Today, be gentle with someone who sees a hard question differently. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics today recognize the Roman line of popes from the schism years as the legitimate one, while honoring saints from both sides, and they pray for Christian unity, especially in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January.

notes: Week end (days 820–826): the carry looks back over the week.
Per the claims rule, the index hook's 'forty confusing years' is not stated; no counts of claimants are given ('rival popes', 'one more claimant than before').

Historical claims to confirm: Roman crowds pressing for a Roman or Italian pope at the conclave; some of the same cardinals later declaring the election forced and electing Clement VII, who settled at Avignon; Catherine backing Urban VI; Vincent Ferrer backing the Avignon line (Benedict XIII) for years before withdrawing support; Pisa's election adding a claimant; Constance: Gregory XII resigned, the others deposed, Martin V elected.
'The Church does not treat ordinary believers of that time as guilty for choosing wrong' is a general statement of the Church's view; confirm phrasing.
Fork reveal says 'ordinary believers had to follow the leaders near them in good faith' — a generalization; confirm.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of John 17:21. howItsDone: Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (January 18–25).
